newsitem.title: USA: Gore lashes clinic bombers; abortion foes march.
newsitem.headline: Gore lashes clinic bombers; abortion foes march.

text.p: Vice President Al Gore lashed out on Wednesday at "terrorists" who attack abortion clinics, as opponents rallied near the White House on the anniversary of the Supreme Court ruling legalising abortion.
Days after bombings at family planning clinics in Atlanta and in Tulsa, Oklahoma, Gore said those responsible would be punished "to the fullest extent of the law."

"To those who committed the horrible deeds of Atlanta and Tulsa ... I say, the American people will not tolerate your cowardly crusade," Gore said in a podium-pounding speech to the National Abortion and Reproductive Rights Action League.
Gore called the clinic bombers "terrorists" who would be found and would not be allowed to "deface our constitution."

Early in the day a tiny explosion close to the hotel where Gore spoke, and not far from an abortion clinic, prompted a security scare but police said it had the force of a firecracker and seemed unrelated to anti-abortion protests.
Gore called on the abortion rights group to acknowledge possible common ground, notably in the area of family planning and education, that might be found with abortion opponents.
But he said: "Regardless of our views on this issue ... we will not allow a woman's right to choose to be taken away."

First lady Hillary Rodham Clinton also addressed the group, expressing her concern for abortion rights and repeating President Bill Clinton's formulation that abortion should be "safe, legal and rare."
She added: "This is never an easy issue and anyone who thinks they have the ultimate truth on this is ... wrong."

Even as they spoke, thousands of abortion opponents gathered at the Ellipse just south of the White House to mark the 24th anniversary of the Supreme Court's ruling in Roe v. Wade, which recognised American women's right to abortion.
Several congressmen told the crowd they would seek to pass a ban on so-called partial-birth abortion, a controversial late-term procedure. Clinton vetoed the measure last year.

"Dear Mr. President ... A generation of kids both here and abroad are at risk because of you," Representative Chris Smith, a New Jersey Republican, told the rally. "Millions have been butchered on your watch."
The president was the target of numerous signs that mocked his statements that abortion should be safe, legal and rare.
"Abortion will be rare: Clinocchio," declared one banner alongside a picture of Clinton looking like Pinocchio with a long nose. "Hey Bill, what if your mom didn't want you?" another sign read.
After the rally, anti-abortion activists marched through downtown Washington to the Supreme Court.

On an anniversary that has become a traditional flashpoint for partisans on all sides of the abortion debate, the U.S. Catholic Conference called on Clinton to discuss the matter with their representative and a "knowledgeable physician."
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott on Tuesday listed the partial-birth abortion ban as one of his Republican party's top legislative priorities in the new congressional session.
But NARAL president Kate Michelman said the right to this kind of abortion, under attack in the Republican-led Congress, would likely be preserved.
Both the National Organisation for Women, which favours abortion rights, and the legal arm of the anti-abortion movement, Americans United for Life, decried violence against clinics.
There were bombings January 16 at a clinic in Atlanta and on Sunday at a Tulsa clinic. No injuries were reported.

In Brookline, Massachusetts, where a gunman killed two receptionists and wounded five others in shootings at two clinics in 1994, security was tightened due to the anniversary and recent attacks elsewhere.
